claim:cat-catch-and-avoid.proposition:
The agent catches circles (mean final distance 0.15, caught at all offsets) and
avoids diamonds (mean final distance 29.6) — a category gap > 8.
claim:cat-catch-and-avoid.hypothesis:
The agent ends close to circles (within the catch radius) and far from diamonds
at every trained offset (−6..+6), a clean behavioural categorization.

claim:cat-categorization-map.proposition:
Circles and diamonds form two separated bands across −8..+6 (catch vs avoid);
the separation collapses at offset ≥7 (untrained), an honest generalization edge.
claim:cat-categorization-map.hypothesis:
Across offsets the circle curve stays near zero (caught) and the diamond curve
stays high (avoided), giving two well-separated bands — Beer's categorization
plot — though generalization may fail past the trained range.

claim:cat-decision-dynamics.proposition:
The coupled neural dynamics commit differently to the two categories: outputs
and the motor-neuron phase trajectory diverge after a shared initial phase.
claim:cat-decision-dynamics.hypothesis:
The neuron-output trajectories (and the motor-neuron phase trajectory) start
together and then separate by category, showing that the decision is a
divergence in the coupled system's state over time, not a discrete switch.

narrative.question:
Can an evolved CTRNN agent, embodied with a fan of ray distance sensors and a
horizontal effector, perceptually categorize falling objects by shape —
catching circles while avoiding diamonds — purely through the dynamics of its
coupled brain–body–environment system, with no internal "shape" label?

decisions.title: Report the ±7–8 avoid-generalization failure as a boundary finding, or re-evolve with wider training offsets?
decisions.detail: Diamonds at offset ≥7 (beyond the ±6 training range) are caught, not avoided. Current framing reports it honestly as a generalization edge.
